title: Gateless Barrier, Case 48: Kan-feng's One Road
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher encourages listeners to examine their approach to spiritual practice, considering whether they are making conscious choices or simply following habits and conditioning. They suggest that even small moments, like daily routines, require intention and attention to stay on track with one's spiritual goals. By recognizing our own wholeness and inner wisdom, we can cultivate a sense of community and mutual support among peers, creating a space where individuals can support each other in their practice.

None of us would ever have made this up, right?
If you're asking, how could I have a deeper, richer life, connect deeply with others, release from negative habit patterns and karma, and find liberation?

Never, never in a million years.

It's good to just over and over again encounter obscure religious literature and notice how, if you find enough support and a little structure and patience, and just stay with it for a while, more is revealed, right?
More is revealed, more and more is revealed.

Case 48.
*A monk asked Ganfeng, a master Ganfeng, "It is written, Buddhas are in the ten directions, but one straight road to Nirvana.
I wonder where that road can be."*
Let me start over.
*A monk asked master Ganfeng, "It is written, Buddhas are in the ten directions, but one straight road to Nirvana.
I wonder where that road can be."*
*Ganfeng lifted up his staff*
(there's another staff story)
*and drew a line and said, "Here it is, here it is."
Later the monks asked the same question to Yunmen, who held up his fan and said, "This fan jumps up to the thirty-third heaven and hits the nose of the deity Sakra Devanam, Indra.
When you strike the carp of the eastern sea, the rain comes down in torrents."*
Here we have another part one, part two koan about a teaching point, and these are different times and different places, jammed in here.
In part one, the main part, the first teacher, Ganfeng, must have just given a talk in which he offered this quotation: Buddhas in the ten directions, but one straight road to Nirvana.
I don't know where that's from.
But in other words, everything is Buddha.
The ten directions represents absolutely everyone in the universe.
Everything is worthy of our attention and our care.
Everything is teaching us.
But, one straight road to Nirvana.
One path.
So this teacher taught all of this, but the monk apparently didn't get it, because he wanted to, he knows what his motivations were.
So he got up at the end of the talk and said this.
You just said it, basically.
You just said, it is written, Buddhas in the ten directions, but one straight road to Nirvana.
Where is that road?
I wonder where that road can be.
So of this vast reality, and this incredibly rich and unknowable life, do we go this way or that way?
Which way do we go?
Where should our focus be?
Where should our attention be?
And the teacher in answer lifted up his staff and drew a line in the air, maybe meaning, here it is.
Right in front of you.
Didn't say anything.
I'm constantly rattling on.
These guys were a little more restrained.
Then sometime later, part two of this story, maybe years later, it doesn't say, in another monastery, monks asked the great teacher Yunmen, whom we've seen in several cases.
He's featured in one of my most favorite ones, about why do you put on the seven-panel robe at the sound of the bell?
That's Yunmen.
And he doesn't just do the nice, simple waving his stick around.
He uses an object.
So objects have power, right?
He held up a fan.

And then he gave this really far-out, complicated thing about the heaven of the 33 and a god named Sacra Devenam and carp in the Eastern Sea, and all these things have all kinds of symbolisms in Buddhism and Chinese culture.
And the rains pour down.
I think for all purposes, we're going to just let that one rest.
We don't need to unpack that.
One could.
That's also a famous part of the tradition.
We could spend a few hours unpacking such a thing, but I don't know if it would be that useful to us.
The main point is useful.
Life is complicated.
Where are you going, right?
What's your intention?
Who are you?
What are you doing?
How do you approach the practice?
The Buddhas are in ten directions.
I mean, there are Buddhas everywhere.
So everyone is Buddha and everything is Buddha, even things that look messed up to us, right?
So how do we navigate all these choices?
And are we even navigating these choices?
Are we even choosing which way to go?
Or are we letting the choice be made for us from habit or conditioning, or doing what somebody else said we were supposed to do, or who knows what?
Are we actually in choice?
Because I think the first question that this koan brings up, that the monk is actually asking, is actually pretty interesting.
In the monastery, it was probably pretty clear what you're supposed to do.
These monasteries were very rule-based.
And I think I mentioned this before, the Zen monasteries, their dharma came largely from the actual living in the monastery, from each thing they did being a moment of practice.
So the rules and regulations are very complicated.

How do we help each other practice the paramitas, practice living mindfully, living in the way we want to live?

A lot is exchanged.
A lot is given.
A lot is received.

We don't always hold it out on our sleeves exactly.

One of them I think about is this wonderful Jungian model.

One of the ways to look at that is that the student is seeking somebody else to tell them they're okay, right?
That's a shallow interpretation.
Oh, would you tell me that I'm okay?
And I'm happy to do that.
But actually, this Jungian model suggests there's a deeper thing that happens, which is that this person is completely whole.
They are Buddha, so the Jungians and the Buddhists agree here, but they can't see it.
They can't feel it, and it's too heavy for them to hold.
So what they're doing is giving the teacher their gold, giving their teacher their gold.

Oh, thank you for being here.
It's really nice to meet you.
Tell me about yourself.
I hope the practice is helpful to you.
And that's just to pass the time, while the teacher's getting a sense of the weight of their gold and deciding where to put it.

Which is that the person, the student in this case, and we think of students and teachers as much more mixed together, but this is simplifying so we can talk, so the teacher grows.
I mean, the student practices and benefits and attends to things and works on stuff.
Maybe they're doing other healthy things for themselves to grow and develop, and eventually they're ready for the gold back.

And so this is why we need the teacher, and this is why when we do this for each other, we need all to be aware that this is happening, that we're depending on each other in these subtle ways to hold for us, each other.
So when the teacher received that gold, the teacher has to know that they received it, not just like, oh, what was that, and drop it somewhere.

So that means they're ready for their gold back, so the teacher better have it handy, and help them understand.
You don't have to burst their bubble, right?

Just fire that teacher.

So I don't know if that's a helpful model, but I thought we'd break into small groups here and just muse together.
How do we support each other in practice as Sangha members?
Are there things we should do?
Should we?
Gee, I don't have your number.
Can we talk every other Sunday?
Check in?

Is it more of a feeling for each of us to carry and remember in our hearts?
And subtle doesn't mean it's not powerful.
Doesn't mean it's not important.
How do we hold gold and share gold and be gold together as a community?
And maybe the conversation can orient around the six paramitas.
How do we do wise generosity with each other?
Lots of opportunities to help each other out, right?
How do we wisely support each other in being ethical, being upright, being the best person we can be?
How do we support each other in wise patience, wise energy, wise concentration?
I guess wise wisdom.
